chapter: Sansu, Irma, Lee Dorsey and the Meters
title: Irma Thomas and feeling in singing
summary: He says a singer need not have lived the pain theoretically, calling Irma's feeling earthy.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: Just as you have to have somebody who's fun to work with for songs like Holy Cow and working on a coal mine, do you think that for someone like Irma Thomas and for blues, to get that really real sound that somebody has to have had a certain amount of real pain in their life and be singing that out? Because you don't hear that in a lot of California white musicians today. It's just that they kind of hit rhythm and blues, but they miss something. I don't know if I have all of that question. Okay. Do you think just as it's important for somebody to put out a fun song, to actually have enjoyed it, do you think that for somebody to put out something like Irma Thomas, like Wish Someone Would Care, that they've got to have been there at some point in their life?
But to come across the way the song was designed to be, theoretically it sounds right that you should have been there.
You had to go through those feelings.

I do say theoretically because there's something about people that work hard at things that I can't overlook. And I've seen some little youngsters that hasn't been around long enough to have been through too much, and they sing with so much like Michael Jackson. I hear more feelings in him sometimes than an 80-year-old man.

But in a case like in Irma, there's so much about Irma's life that is so earthy. The first thing about Irma is it's earthy. It's definitely earthy. Then now what? So I think the difference in, I would rather define it as being more earthy than that you have to have been in certain places to. I hope that makes some sort of sense.
